claim: Language is sustained by large-scale networks in the human brain.
source: Language is sustained by large-scale networks in the human brain.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about language organization in the brain.

claim: Stroke often severely affects function and network dynamics.
source: Stroke often severely affects function and network dynamics.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about stroke effects on brain function.

claim: Perturbation of the posterior IFG selectively delayed phonological decisions.
source: Perturbation of the posterior IFG selectively delayed phonological decisions and decreased phonological activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Perturbation of the posterior IFG decreased phonological activity.
source: Perturbation of the posterior IFG selectively delayed phonological decisions and decreased phonological activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data presented in the study.

claim: The individual response delay was correlated with the upregulation of the lesion homologue, likely reflecting compensation.
source: The individual response delay was correlated with the upregulation of the lesion homologue, likely reflecting compensation.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between behavioral and fMRI data, with an interpretation about compensation.

claim: Stronger individual tract integrity of the right superior longitudinal fascicle was associated with lesser disruption.
source: Moreover, stronger individual tract integrity of the right superior longitudinal fascicle was associated with lesser disruption.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between DTI measures and behavioral data.

claim: Recent work considers aphasia a network disorder, emphasizing the importance of disturbed interactions between key areas.
source: Accordingly, recent work considers aphasia a network disorder, emphasizing the importance of disturbed interactions between key areas (Corbetta et al., 2015; Fridriksson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some studies found that early upregulation of the right hemisphere was beneficial for aphasia recovery.
source: Some studies found that (early) upregulation of the right hemisphere was beneficial for aphasia recovery (e.g. Crinion and Price, 2005; Robson et al., 2014; Saur et al., 2006; Weiller et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Other results showed that upregulation of the right hemisphere reflected maladaptive changes in patients with non-fluent aphasia.
source: In contrast, other results showed that such upregulation reflected maladaptive changes in patients with non-fluent aphasia (e.g. Heiss et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2005; Naeser et al., 2005; Naeser et al., 2011; Postman-Caucheteux et al., 2010; Rosen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Suppression of right-hemispheric 'overactivation' with inhibitory transcranial magnetic stimulation in patients with post-stroke aphasia after left-hemispheric lesions resulted in improved language production.
source: Accordingly, suppression of right-hemispheric 'overactivation' with inhibitory transcranial magnetic stimulation in patients with post-stroke aphasia after left-hemispheric lesions resulted in improved language production (e.g. Barwood et al., 2013; Naeser et al., 2005; Naeser et al., 2011; Weiduschat et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Language reorganization appears to be a dynamic process and the contribution of the right hemisphere may change across the time course of recovery.
source: Indeed, language reorganization appears to be a dynamic process and the contribution of the right hemisphere may change across the time course of recovery (Hartwigsen and Saur, 2019; Saur et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Virtual lesions provide a well-controlled approach to study short-term reorganization at the neural network level unconfounded by long-term recovery.
source: Virtual lesions provide a well-controlled approach to study short-term reorganization at the neural network level unconfounded by long-term recovery (Siebner and Rothwell, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Phonological processing relies on the posterior inferior frontal gyrus (pIFG) and supramarginal gyrus (SMG).
source: Specifically, aside from temporal regions, phonological processing relies on the posterior inferior frontal gyrus (pIFG) and supramarginal gyrus (SMG) (Devlin et al., 2003; Poldrack et al., 1999; Price et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging research.

claim: Semantic processing consistently engages anterior inferior frontal gyrus (aIFG), anterior temporal lobe (ATL), posterior middle temporal gyrus (pMTG), and angular gyrus (AG).
source: In contrast, semantic processing consistently engages anterior inferior frontal gyrus (aIFG), anterior temporal lobe (ATL), posterior middle temporal gyrus (pMTG), and angular gyrus (AG) (Binder et al., 2009; Devlin et al., 2003; Vigneau et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging research.

claim: Studies on patients with structural lesions provided evidence for a key contribution of distinct parietal and frontal regions to phonological and semantic processing.
source: In line with these results, studies on patients with structural lesions provided evidence for a key contribution of distinct parietal and frontal regions to phonological and semantic processing (Corbett et al., 2009; Dewarrat et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous lesion studies.

claim: Neurostimulation studies using inhibitory transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) demonstrated the functional relevance of left pIFG and SMG for phonological processing.
source: In a similar vein, neurostimulation studies using inhibitory transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), demonstrated the functional relevance of left pIFG and SMG for phonological processing (Gough et al., 2005; Hartwigsen et al., 2010; Oberhuber et al., 2016; Romero et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous TMS studies.

claim: rTMS studies showed that the left aIFG, ATL, pMTG and AG contribute to semantic processing.
source: Other rTMS studies further showed that the left aIFG, ATL, pMTG and AG contribute to semantic processing (Binney and Ralph, 2015; Davey et al., 2015; Gough et al., 2005; Jung and Lambon Ralph, 2016; Whitney et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous TMS studies.

claim: Phonological and semantic processing are integrated in two segregated functional-anatomic networks that connect inferior parietal and inferior frontal regions.
source: Based on these findings, we recently combined different inhibitory rTMS protocols over selected inferior frontal and parietal regions to demonstrate that phonological and semantic processing are integrated in two segregated functional-anatomic networks that connect inferior parietal and inferior frontal regions (Hartwigsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous research.

claim: TMS-induced disruption of left AG or SMG in the healthy brain resulted in large-scale inhibitory effects and increased the functional interaction between phonological and semantic networks.
source: Moreover, TMS-induced disruption of left AG or SMG in the healthy brain resulted in large-scale inhibitory effects and increased the functional interaction between these networks (Hartwigsen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous research.

claim: 12 right-handed native German-speaking patients with a single chronic embolic stroke completed the study.
source: 12 right-handed native German-speaking patients with a single chronic embolic stroke (mean age: 58.8 years, range: 43–72 years) and no history of other neurological disorders or TMS contraindications completed our study.
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: Patients were selected based on their lesion site, including the left (temporo-)parietal cortex while leaving the frontal cortex intact.
source: Patients were selected based on their lesion site, including the left (temporo-)parietal cortex while leaving the frontal cortex intact (Figure 2A and Table 1).
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the study sample, with reference to figure and table.

claim: All patients were in the chronic phase after stroke (>6 months, mean 37.9, SD = 34.8 months).
source: All patients were in the chronic phase after stroke (>6 months, mean 37.9, SD = 34.8 months) and initially presented with aphasia but showed (almost) complete language recovery at the time of the experiment.
evidence: This describes the time since stroke for the study sample.

claim: 7 patients were diagnosed with residual aphasia, and the remaining 5 patients had no residual aphasia at time of participation.
source: Specifically, 7 patients were diagnosed with residual aphasia, and the remaining 5 patients had no residual aphasia at time of participation (range, 6 to 122 months post-stroke, see Table 1).
evidence: This describes the language status of the study sample.

claim: The interaction between task and cTBS was significant (F2,22 = 8.59, p=0.002).
source: Accordingly, the interaction between task and cTBS was significant (F2,22 = 8.59, p=0.002).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: cTBS over pIFG significantly delayed phonological response times when compared against cTBS over aIFG (t11 = 3.19, p=0.002).
source: Bonferroni-Holm corrected post-hoc paired t-tests showed that cTBS over pIFG significantly delayed phonological response times when compared against cTBS over aIFG (t11 = 3.19, p=0.002) or sham cTBS (t11 = 2.99, p=0.009).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: cTBS over pIFG significantly delayed phonological response times when compared against sham cTBS (t11 = 2.99, p=0.009).
source: Bonferroni-Holm corrected post-hoc paired t-tests showed that cTBS over pIFG significantly delayed phonological response times when compared against cTBS over aIFG (t11 = 3.19, p=0.002) or sham cTBS (t11 = 2.99, p=0.009).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in phonological response times for aIFG and sham cTBS (p=0.95).
source: There was no significant difference in phonological response times for aIFG and sham cTBS (p=0.95).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Semantic response speed was significantly prolonged with cTBS over aIFG relative to cTBS over pIFG (t11 = 2.89, p=0.01).
source: In contrast, semantic response speed was significantly prolonged with cTBS over aIFG relative to cTBS over pIFG (t11 = 2.89, p=0.01) or sham cTBS (t11 = 2.23, p=0.048, does not survive a Bonferroni-Holm correction).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Semantic response speed was significantly prolonged with cTBS over aIFG relative to sham cTBS (t11 = 2.23, p=0.048, does not survive a Bonferroni-Holm correction).
source: In contrast, semantic response speed was significantly prolonged with cTBS over aIFG relative to cTBS over pIFG (t11 = 2.89, p=0.01) or sham cTBS (t11 = 2.23, p=0.048, does not survive a Bonferroni-Holm correction).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis, though it does not survive correction for multiple comparisons.

claim: A main effect of task (F1,11 = 30.77, p=0.0001) revealed overall longer response times for phonological than semantic decisions independent of the cTBS condition.
source: Additionally, a main effect of task (F1,11 = 30.77, p=0.0001) revealed overall longer response times for phonological than semantic decisions independent of the cTBS condition.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: A main effect of cTBS (F2,22 = 4.20, p=0.028) showed overall differences between the cTBS conditions with the strongest impact of cTBS over pIFG on task performance.
source: Finally, a main effect of cTBS (F2,22 = 4.20, p=0.028) showed overall differences between the cTBS conditions with the strongest impact of cTBS over pIFG on task performance (post-hoc t-test only significant for pIFG >sham cTBS: t11 = 2.08; p=0.048, does not survive a Bonferroni-Holm correction; pIFG >aIFG cTBS: p=0.13; aIFG >sham cTBS: p=0.33).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: No significant differences in error rates were found (all p>0.05).
source: We did not find any significant differences in error rates (all p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: During both tasks, patients showed increased activity in a large network of bilateral brain regions, mainly in the frontal cortex, that were previously associated with task effort and language comprehension.
source: During both tasks, patients showed increased activity in a large network of bilateral brain regions, mainly in the frontal cortex, that were previously associated with task effort and language comprehension (Price, 2010).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis with reference to previous literature.

claim: During phonological decisions, the comparison of cTBS over pIFG relative to sham cTBS showed a strong decrease of task-related activity in the targeted region (left pIFG: x, y, z = −54, 12, 17; T = 4.97).
source: Specifically, during phonological decisions, the comparison of cTBS over pIFG relative to sham cTBS showed a strong decrease of task-related activity in the targeted region (left pIFG: x, y, z = −54, 12, 17; T = 4.97; Figure 4A), as well as in the supplementary motor area (x, y, z = 1, 3, 54; T = 4.90) and in the right putamen (x, y, z = 18, 6,–7; T = 4.80).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: cTBS over pIFG relative to sham cTBS decreased task-related activity in the supplementary motor area (x, y, z = 1, 3, 54; T = 4.90) during phonological decisions.
source: Specifically, during phonological decisions, the comparison of cTBS over pIFG relative to sham cTBS showed a strong decrease of task-related activity in the targeted region (left pIFG: x, y, z = −54, 12, 17; T = 4.97; Figure 4A), as well as in the supplementary motor area (x, y, z = 1, 3, 54; T = 4.90) and in the right putamen (x, y, z = 18, 6,–7; T = 4.80).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: cTBS over pIFG relative to sham cTBS decreased task-related activity in the right putamen (x, y, z = 18, 6,–7; T = 4.80) during phonological decisions.
source: Specifically, during phonological decisions, the comparison of cTBS over pIFG relative to sham cTBS showed a strong decrease of task-related activity in the targeted region (left pIFG: x, y, z = −54, 12, 17; T = 4.97; Figure 4A), as well as in the supplementary motor area (x, y, z = 1, 3, 54; T = 4.90) and in the right putamen (x, y, z = 18, 6,–7; T = 4.80).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: The comparison of cTBS over pIFG relative to cTBS of aIFG revealed decrease of task-related activity in the stimulated area (left pIFG: x, y, z = −54, 23, 18; T = 4.92) during phonological decisions.
source: Likewise, the comparison of cTBS over pIFG relative to cTBS of aIFG also revealed decrease of task-related activity in the stimulated area (left pIFG: x, y, z = −54, 23, 18; T = 4.92).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: Compared with sham cTBS, cTBS over aIFG resulted in a strong decrease in task-related activity in the left aIFG (x, y, z = −36, 31,–1; T = 4.80) during semantic decisions.
source: Compared with sham cTBS, cTBS over aIFG resulted in a strong decrease in task-related activity in a larger network of frontal brain areas, including the left aIFG (x, y, z = −36, 31,–1; T = 4.80; Figure 4B), left middle frontal gyrus (x, y, z = −45, 35, 26; T = 4.78) and a number of right-hemispheric frontal regions, including the middle frontal gyrus (x, y, z = 45, 35, 32; T = 5.20), superior frontal gyrus (x, y, z = 9, 35, 41; T = 4.99) and the homologous aIFG region (right aIFG: x, y, z = 40, 37, 3; T = 4.90).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Compared with sham cTBS, cTBS over aIFG resulted in a strong decrease in task-related activity in the left middle frontal gyrus (x, y, z = −45, 35, 26; T = 4.78) during semantic decisions.
source: Compared with sham cTBS, cTBS over aIFG resulted in a strong decrease in task-related activity in a larger network of frontal brain areas, including the left aIFG (x, y, z = −36, 31,–1; T = 4.80; Figure 4B), left middle frontal gyrus (x, y, z = −45, 35, 26; T = 4.78) and a number of right-hemispheric frontal regions, including the middle frontal gyrus (x, y, z = 45, 35, 32; T = 5.20), superior frontal gyrus (x, y, z = 9, 35, 41; T = 4.99) and the homologous aIFG region (right aIFG: x, y, z = 40, 37, 3; T = 4.90).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: Compared with sham cTBS, cTBS over aIFG resulted in a strong decrease in task-related activity in the right middle frontal gyrus (x, y, z = 45, 35, 32; T = 5.20) during semantic decisions.
source: Compared with sham cTBS, cTBS over aIFG resulted in a strong decrease in task-related activity in a larger network of frontal brain areas, including the left aIFG (x, y, z = −36, 31,–1; T = 4.80; Figure 4B), left middle frontal gyrus (x, y, z = −45, 35, 26; T = 4.78) and a number of right-hemispheric frontal regions, including the middle frontal gyrus (x, y, z = 45, 35, 32; T = 5.20), superior frontal gyrus (x, y, z = 9, 35, 41; T = 4.99) and the homologous aIFG region (right aIFG: x, y, z = 40, 37, 3; T = 4.90).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: Compared with sham cTBS, cTBS over aIFG resulted in a strong decrease in task-related activity in the right superior frontal gyrus (x, y, z = 9, 35, 41; T = 4.99) during semantic decisions.
source: Compared with sham cTBS, cTBS over aIFG resulted in a strong decrease in task-related activity in a larger network of frontal brain areas, including the left aIFG (x, y, z = −36, 31,–1; T = 4.80; Figure 4B), left middle frontal gyrus (x, y, z = −45, 35, 26; T = 4.78) and a number of right-hemispheric frontal regions, including the middle frontal gyrus (x, y, z = 45, 35, 32; T = 5.20), superior frontal gyrus (x, y, z = 9, 35, 41; T = 4.99) and the homologous aIFG region (right aIFG: x, y, z = 40, 37, 3; T = 4.90).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: Compared with sham cTBS, cTBS over aIFG resulted in a strong decrease in task-related activity in the right aIFG (x, y, z = 40, 37, 3; T = 4.90) during semantic decisions.
source: Compared with sham cTBS, cTBS over aIFG resulted in a strong decrease in task-related activity in a larger network of frontal brain areas, including the left aIFG (x, y, z = −36, 31,–1; T = 4.80; Figure 4B), left middle frontal gyrus (x, y, z = −45, 35, 26; T = 4.78) and a number of right-hemispheric frontal regions, including the middle frontal gyrus (x, y, z = 45, 35, 32; T = 5.20), superior frontal gyrus (x, y, z = 9, 35, 41; T = 4.99) and the homologous aIFG region (right aIFG: x, y, z = 40, 37, 3; T = 4.90).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: No brain regions showed significantly increased task-related activity after cTBS over either the aIFG or pIFG during semantic or phonological processing.
source: We did not find any brain regions that showed significantly increased task-related activity after cTBS over either the aIFG or pIFG during semantic or phonological processing.
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: The delay in phonological response speed was positively correlated with the individual upregulation of the right SMG and adjacent postcentral gyrus (x, y, z = 54,–19, 29; T = 6.53) after cTBS over pIFG relative to sham cTBS.
source: We found that the delay in phonological response speed was positively correlated with the individual upregulation of the right SMG and adjacent postcentral gyrus (x, y, z = 54,–19, 29; T = 6.53) after cTBS over pIFG relative to sham cTBS (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on regression analysis of fMRI and behavioral data with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The correlation between phonological response delay and right SMG upregulation remained significant after adjusting for the lesion volume.
source: Note that this effect remained significant after adjusting for the lesion volume.
evidence: This is based on regression analysis controlling for lesion volume.

claim: Patients who had the strongest delay in phonological response speed after cTBS over pIFG showed the strongest upregulation of the contralesional right SMG, likely in an attempt to compensate for the cTBS-induced disruption of the phonological system.
source: This shows that those patients who had the strongest delay in phonological response speed after cTBS over pIFG showed the strongest upregulation of the contralesional right SMG, likely in an attempt to compensate for the cTBS-induced disruption of the phonological system.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation data with speculation about compensatory mechanisms.

claim: No significant correlation was found for semantic decisions.
source: We did not find any significant correlation for semantic decisions.
evidence: This is based on regression analysis of fMRI and behavioral data.

claim: The individual FA for the right SLF was negatively correlated with the relative increase in the individual mean reaction times for the phonological task after cTBS of pIFG relative to sham cTBS (R2 = 0.42; p=0.02; two-tailed).
source: Indeed, we found a significant negative relationship, indicating that patients who had a stronger tract integrity of the right SLF were less affected by the virtual lesion and might thus have shown a better compensation by recruiting processing resources in the right SMG via the intact right SLF (R2 = 0.42; p=0.02; two-tailed; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between DTI and behavioral data with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Patients who had a stronger tract integrity of the right SLF were less affected by the virtual lesion and might thus have shown a better compensation by recruiting processing resources in the right SMG via the intact right SLF.
source: Indeed, we found a significant negative relationship, indicating that patients who had a stronger tract integrity of the right SLF were less affected by the virtual lesion and might thus have shown a better compensation by recruiting processing resources in the right SMG via the intact right SLF (R2 = 0.42; p=0.02; two-tailed; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation data with speculation about compensatory mechanisms.

claim: There was no correlation between phonological response delay and fractional anisotropy in the neighboring IFOF (all p>0.05).
source: This effect was anatomically and functionally specific as there was no correlation between phonological response delay and fractional anisotropy in the neighboring IFOF, or between tract integrity and semantic response delay (all p>0.05).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between DTI and behavioral data.

claim: There was no correlation between tract integrity and semantic response delay (all p>0.05).
source: This effect was anatomically and functionally specific as there was no correlation between phonological response delay and fractional anisotropy in the neighboring IFOF, or between tract integrity and semantic response delay (all p>0.05).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between DTI and behavioral data.

claim: This study represents the first investigation of short-term reorganization in the lesioned language network.
source: This study represents the first investigation of short-term reorganization in the lesioned language network.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The results provide evidence for a functional-anatomical double dissociation in the left IFG.
source: Our results provide evidence for a functional-anatomical double dissociation in the left IFG.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the behavioral and fMRI findings.

claim: The observed correlation between cTBS-induced response delay and upregulation of the lesion homologue most likely reflects partial compensation by recruitment of a right hemisphere area.
source: Consequently, we believe that the observed correlation between cTBS-induced response delay and upregulation of the lesion homologue most likely reflects partial compensation by recruitment of a right hemisphere area.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation data.

claim: The results speak for an adaptive contribution of the right hemisphere, at least with respect to short-term adaptation for phonological processing in patients with left temporo-parietal lesions.
source: While the role of the right hemisphere in language recovery after stroke remains highly controversial, our results speak for an adaptive contribution, at least with respect to short-term adaptation for phonological processing in patients with left temporo-parietal lesions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: A beneficial role of right-hemispheric regions in language recovery after stroke was suggested in a number of previous studies.
source: Indeed, a beneficial role of right-hemispheric regions in language recovery after stroke was suggested in a number of previous studies (Hamilton et al., 2011; Saur et al., 2006; Turkeltaub, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increased activity in a large network of bilateral frontal regions was already observed after sham cTBS in the study.
source: Accordingly, increased activity in a large network of bilateral frontal regions was already observed after sham cTBS in our study.
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: The observed task-specific recruitment of brain regions after sham cTBS was largely similar to that observed in a previous study on healthy volunteers that used the same tasks and comparisons, except for the absence of any activity in left temporo-parietal regions in the present study.
source: Note that the observed task-specific recruitment of brain regions after sham cTBS was largely similar to that observed in our previous study on healthy volunteers that used the same tasks and comparisons (Hartwigsen et al., 2017), except for the absence of any activity in left temporo-parietal regions in the present study that can be explained by the lesion site in our sample of patients.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous research by the authors.

claim: The virtual lesion of the pIFG unmasked the contribution of the right SMG to phonological decisions.
source: A likely explanation for these findings is that the virtual lesion of the pIFG unmasked the contribution of the right SMG to phonological decisions (see Sack et al., 2005 for a similar ratio).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with reference to a similar concept in previous research.

claim: The lesioned network preserves its flexibility to partially compensate for a focal perturbation of a key region in the left-hemispheric language network.
source: These results are noteworthy because they show that the lesioned network preserves its flexibility to partially compensate for a focal perturbation of a key region in the left-hemispheric language network.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: Compensatory increases in right temporo-parietal activity after left temporo-parietal lesions were not observed in a recent longitudinal study on language recovery after stroke.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe compensatory increases in right temporo-parietal activity after left temporo-parietal lesions in our recent longitudinal study on language recovery after stroke (Stockert et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous research by the authors.

claim: The additional TMS-induced perturbation of the left frontal cortex in the present study was likely necessary to unmask the role of the right hemisphere.
source: It is likely that the additional TMS-induced perturbation of the left frontal cortex in the present study was necessary to unmask the role of the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is speculation about why the current findings differ from previous research.

claim: If the findings mainly reflected a disinhibition, resulting from a cTBS-induced reduction in the transcallosal inhibition from the left to the right hemisphere, then one would have expected a strong upregulation of the stimulation homologue in the right posterior IFG.
source: First, if our findings mainly reflected a disinhibition, resulting from a cTBS-induced reduction in the transcallosal inhibition from the left to the right hemisphere, then one would have expected a strong upregulation of the stimulation homologue in the right posterior IFG.
evidence: This is a logical argument against an alternative interpretation.

claim: A maladaptive role of the right hemisphere would not be congruent with the observed positive correlation between the individual tract integrity in the right SLF and the individual performance in the phonological task.
source: Secondly, a maladaptive role of the right hemisphere would not be congruent with the observed positive correlation between the individual tract integrity in the right SLF and the individual performance in the phonological task, linking stronger tract integrity with a stronger resilience of the phonological network.
evidence: This is a logical argument against an alternative interpretation based on the data.

claim: A previous study in healthy volunteers showed that TMS-induced perturbation of the right SMG decreased response efficiency in the same syllable judgement task that was used in the present study.
source: Finally, a previous study in healthy volunteers showed that TMS-induced perturbation of the right SMG decreased response efficiency in the same syllable judgement task that was used in the present study, providing evidence for a functional role of the right SMG in phonological (working memory) processes (Hartwigsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: The results speak more in favor of a compensatory role of the right lesion homologue in the parietal cortex.
source: Together, our results speak more in favor of a compensatory role of the right lesion homologue in the parietal cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: Differences in the individual structural network architecture modulate the compensatory potential of the non-dominant hemisphere, enabling large-scale interactions in right-hemispheric homologous language regions.
source: The identified structural predictor of differences in resilience to virtual lesions suggests that differences in the individual structural network architecture modulate the compensatory potential of the non-dominant hemisphere, enabling large-scale interactions in right-hemispheric homologous language regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DTI findings.

claim: A previous study in patients with aphasia after left-hemispheric stroke reported a correlation between increased grey or white matter volume in the contralesional right SMG and preserved speech abilities.
source: This notion is supported by a previous study in patients with aphasia after left-hemispheric stroke that reported a correlation between increased grey or white matter volume in the contralesional right SMG and preserved speech abilities (Balaev et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Premorbid individual variance rather than a compensatory change in white matter integrity after the stroke-induced lesion appears to be the most likely factor that affected the individual ability for short-term compensation.
source: In our study, premorbid individual variance rather than a compensatory change in white matter integrity after the stroke-induced lesion appears to be the most likely factor that affected the individual ability for short-term compensation.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the DTI findings.

claim: The results suggest that with increased task demands (i.e., with large lesions), the facilitation of lesion homologues with non-invasive brain stimulation may be an avenue for therapeutic intervention.
source: Our results suggest that with increased task demands (i.e., with large lesions), the facilitation of lesion homologues with non-invasive brain stimulation may be an avenue for therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This is speculation about potential clinical applications based on the findings.

claim: Right-hemispheric recruitment might become increasingly relevant if the left-hemispheric network lacks the capacity to recover due to large lesions.
source: Indeed, right-hemispheric recruitment might become increasingly relevant if the left-hemispheric network lacks the capacity to recover due to large lesions (Heiss and Thiel, 2006).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Most studies using non-invasive brain stimulation to support language therapy focus on facilitation of perilesional regions or inhibition of contralesional frontal regions.
source: While an increasing number of studies use non-invasive brain stimulation to support language therapy (e.g. Coslett, 2016; Otal et al., 2015), most of these studies focus on facilitation of perilesional regions or inhibition of contralesional frontal regions.
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: Only a few studies applied facilitatory stimulation over right-hemispheric regions.
source: To date, only a few studies applied facilitatory stimulation over right-hemispheric regions (Flöel et al., 2011; Vines et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: Some studies also reported language improvement after inhibition of right hemispheric homologues.
source: However, we wish to emphasize that this might not generalize to all lesion patterns and aphasia types since some studies also reported language improvement after inhibition of right hemispheric homologues (see Naeser et al., 2005; Naeser et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: The beneficial or maladaptive role of the right hemisphere in language recovery may strongly depend on the lesion site (e.g. frontal vs. temporo-parietal stroke) and size and the aphasia type.
source: Indeed, the beneficial or maladaptive role of the right hemisphere in language recovery may strongly depend on the lesion site (e.g. frontal vs. temporo-parietal stroke) and size and the aphasia type (e.g. Heiss and Thiel, 2006; Naeser et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The observed short-term reorganization in the right-hemisphere might be best comparable with an early beneficial recruitment of right-hemispheric language homologues in post-stroke aphasia.
source: The observed short-term reorganization in the right-hemisphere in our study might be best comparable with an early beneficial recruitment of right-hemispheric language homologues in post-stroke aphasia (Saur et al., 2006).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A focal perturbation of the left IFG was sufficient to result in widespread bilateral activity decreases during semantic decisions.
source: The fact that a focal perturbation of the left IFG was sufficient to result in widespread bilateral activity decreases points towards strong remote effects of plasticity-inducing TMS protocols as demonstrated in previous studies in the semantic network (Binney and Ralph, 2015; Hallam et al., 2016; Hartwigsen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data with reference to previous research.

claim: The behavioural disruption in combination with a bilateral inhibition of task-related activity is congruent with previous lesion studies indicating that semantic impairment is often associated with bilateral disruption of semantic key regions.
source: The behavioural disruption in combination with a bilateral inhibition of task-related activity in our study is further congruent with previous lesion studies indicating that semantic impairment is often associated with bilateral disruption of semantic key regions (Bi et al., 2011; Lambon Ralph et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to previous research.

claim: These results speak in favour of a bilateral organization of the (executive) semantic system with densely connected key areas.
source: Together, these results speak in favour of a bilateral organization of the (executive) semantic system with densely connected key areas (Jung and Lambon Ralph, 2016; Thompson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The strong inhibitory network effect is in line with a previous study in healthy volunteers that used a similar task.
source: The strong inhibitory network effect is further in line with our previous study in healthy volunteers that used a similar task (Hartwigsen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous research by the authors.

claim: Previous rTMS studies in healthy volunteers demonstrated increased task-related activity in homologous right-hemispheric regions or neighbouring left-hemispheric regions after perturbation of semantic key regions.
source: However, the absence of compensatory upregulation of other (semantic) network nodes is surprising given that previous rTMS studies in healthy volunteers demonstrated increased task-related activity in homologous right-hemispheric regions (Andoh and Paus, 2011; Jung and Lambon Ralph, 2016) or neighbouring left-hemispheric regions (Hallam et al., 2016; Hartwigsen et al., 2017) after perturbation of semantic key regions.
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: The absence of short-term reorganization is most likely explained by the widespread inhibition effect in both domain-specific semantic and domain-general areas in the frontal cortex.
source: The absence of short-term reorganization in our study is most likely explained by the above-discussed widespread inhibition effect in both domain-specific semantic and domain-general areas in the frontal cortex.
evidence: This is speculation about why the current findings differ from previous research.

claim: The absence of recruitment of the intact ventrolateral ATL might have resulted from the use of a 'standard' fMRI sequence that lacked sensitivity to capture signal changes in the anterior temporal lobe.
source: The absence of its recruitment in our study might have resulted from the use of a 'standard' fMRI sequence that lacked sensitivity to capture signal changes in the anterior temporal lobe (see Halai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about a methodological limitation supported by a citation.

claim: The behavioural perturbation effect on semantic decisions speaks for a global inhibitory network effect, supporting the view that the lesioned language network is more susceptible to virtual lesion effects.
source: In summary, the behavioural perturbation effect on semantic decisions in our patients speaks for a global inhibitory network effect, supporting the view that the lesioned language network is more susceptible to virtual lesion effects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: The findings may indicate that adaptive plasticity after a virtual lesion is qualitatively different in the reorganized language network.
source: Most importantly, our findings may indicate that adaptive plasticity after a virtual lesion is qualitatively different in the reorganized language network.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: The strong effects found in the reorganized language network can be explained by the increased lesion load after the 'double lesion' in the left hemisphere.
source: Hence, it appears likely that the strong effects found in the reorganized language network can be explained by the increased lesion load after the 'double lesion' in the left hemisphere.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: The network challenge induced by a combination of (virtual) lesions has a strong impact on neural activity and behavioural performance.
source: Together, the previous and present results indicate that the network challenge induced by a combination of (virtual) lesions has a strong impact on neural activity and behavioural performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of previous research.

claim: Task accuracy was not significantly impaired by cTBS in either of the two tasks, suggesting some degree of robustness of the reorganized network against the cTBS effect.
source: Despite this increase in the lesion load, task accuracy was not significantly impaired by cTBS in either of the two tasks, suggesting some degree of robustness of the reorganized network against the cTBS effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: Previous studies in healthy participants report behavioural TMS effects on response speed rather than accuracy, suggesting that the TMS-induced 'neural noise' is unlikely to completely 'silence' the targeted area.
source: This converges with previous studies in healthy participants, which report behavioural TMS effects on response speed rather than accuracy, suggesting that the TMS-induced 'neural noise' is unlikely to completely 'silence' the targeted area (Miniussi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous research supported by a citation.

claim: The observed functional-anatomic double dissociation in the tasks is congruent with previous evidence from healthy participants that associated left aIFG with semantic and left pIFG with phonological processing.
source: It should be emphasized that the observed functional-anatomic double dissociation in our tasks is congruent with previous evidence from healthy participants that associated left aIFG with semantic and left pIFG with phonological processing (Gough et al., 2005; Romero et al., 2006; Vigneau et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of previous research.

claim: The task-specific behavioural perturbation effect was underpinned by task-specific inhibition at the respective targeted region that likely represents the neural correlate of the virtual lesion effect.
source: Extending previous findings, we show that the task-specific behavioural perturbation effect was underpinned by task-specific inhibition at the respective targeted region that likely represents the neural correlate of the virtual lesion effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined behavioral and fMRI findings.

claim: All patients underwent two active cTBS conditions and a sham condition, allowing for a complete within-subject design and thus direct comparisons between the different cTBS conditions in the same patients.
source: However, we wish to emphasize that all patients underwent two active cTBS conditions and a sham condition, allowing for a complete within-subject design and thus direct comparisons between the different cTBS conditions in the same patients.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: If the notion of a beneficial role of the right SMG holds true, then more severe language impairment may require a stronger contribution of the right hemisphere.
source: If the notion of a beneficial role of the right SMG holds true, then we would predict that more severe language impairment may require a stronger contribution of the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is speculation about future predictions based on the findings.

claim: Two patients showed the opposite pattern compared to the average of the group (i.e., decreased activity in the right SMG after cTBS over left pIFG relative to sham stimulation) and one of them had faster phonological response speed after cTBS.
source: Notably, two of our patients showed the opposite pattern compared to the average of the group (i.e., decreased activity in the right SMG after cTBS over left pIFG relative to sham stimulation) and one of them had faster phonological response speed after cTBS.
evidence: This describes individual variability in the data.

claim: Both patients who showed the opposite pattern were fully recovered at the time of study and had the overall smallest lesion sizes.
source: Given the small number of observations (2 out of 12), these findings should be taken with caution. Nevertheless, it is interesting to note that both patients were fully recovered at the time of study and had the overall smallest lesion sizes.
evidence: This describes characteristics of specific patients in the sample.

claim: The recruitment of the right hemisphere was restricted to patients with larger lesion sizes and relatively stronger language deficits.
source: While lesion size was included in our fMRI design as a covariate, these findings might suggest that the recruitment of the right hemisphere was restricted to patients with larger lesion sizes and relatively stronger language deficits.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of individual variability in the data.

claim: The study demonstrates task-specific functional reorganization in the lesioned language network.
source: In summary, we demonstrate task-specific functional reorganization in the lesioned language network.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The upregulation of the contralesional right homologue after a 'double lesion' in the language network implicates that increased task demands induced by neuronal network challenges likely require the contribution of right-hemispheric regions.
source: The upregulation of the contralesional right homologue after a 'double lesion' in the language network implicates that increased task demands induced by neuronal network challenges likely require the contribution of right-hemispheric regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the main findings.

claim: The average time between stimulation offset and fMRI onset was 6 min.
source: As the TMS laboratory was situated close to the MR unit, the average time between stimulation offset and fMRI onset was 6 min.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail.

claim: Each fMRI session was divided into two runs with a short break.
source: Each fMRI session was divided into two runs with a short break.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Each session consisted of 10 miniblocks per task, leading to a total presentation of 120 stimuli per session.
source: Each session consisted of 10 miniblocks per task, leading to a total presentation of 120 stimuli per session.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The same stimuli were used in all sessions.
source: The same stimuli were used in all sessions.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Stimuli were taken from a previous study in healthy participants.
source: Stimuli were taken from our previous study in healthy participants (Hartwigsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the source of experimental materials with a citation.

claim: Only highly frequent, unambiguous nouns from the CELEX lexical database for German were included.
source: Only highly frequent, unambiguous nouns from the CELEX lexical database for German (Centre for Lexical Information, Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics, The Netherlands) were included.
evidence: This describes the stimulus selection criteria.

claim: 60 two-syllable nouns and 60 three-syllable nouns were selected.
source: In total, 60 two-syllable nouns and 60 three-syllable nouns were selected.
evidence: This describes the stimulus set.

claim: All words represented natural or man-made items (i.e., 50% of the 2-syllable words and 50% of the 3-syllable words, respectively).
source: All words represented natural or man-made items (i.e., 50% of the 2-syllable words and 50% of the 3-syllable words, respectively).
evidence: This describes the stimulus characteristics.

claim: MRI data were obtained at a 3-Tesla MRI (Siemens Verio; Siemens, Erlangen).
source: MRI data were obtained at a 3-Tesla MRI (Siemens Verio; Siemens, Erlangen).
evidence: This describes the MRI equipment used.

claim: 370 volumes consisting of 38 slices were acquired continuously during each run.
source: 370 volumes consisting of 38 slices were acquired continuously during each run.
evidence: This describes the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: cTBS was performed using the mean MNI coordinates for left aIFG (x, y, z = −45, 27, 12 mm) and pIFG (x, y, z = −47, 6, 21 mm) from a previous rTMS study in healthy volunteers.
source: cTBS was performed using the mean MNI coordinates for left aIFG (x, y, z = −45, 27, 12 mm) and pIFG (x, y, z = −47, 6, 21 mm) from our previous rTMS study in healthy volunteers (Hartwigsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the TMS targeting method with a citation.

claim: A stimulation intensity of 80% of the individual active motor threshold (AMT) was used.
source: We used a stimulation intensity of 80% of the individual active motor threshold (AMT).
evidence: This describes the TMS intensity.

claim: AMT was defined as the lowest stimulus intensity producing a motor evoked potential of 150–200 μV in the tonically active first dorsal interosseus muscle (20% of maximum contraction).
source: AMT was defined as the lowest stimulus intensity producing a motor evoked potential of 150–200 μV in the tonically active first dorsal interosseus muscle (20% of maximum contraction).
evidence: This describes the method for determining TMS intensity.

claim: For sham cTBS, a figure-of-eight shaped placebo coil was used that creates an identical sound level but provides an effective field reduction of 80%.
source: For sham cTBS, we used a figure-of-eight shaped placebo coil that creates an identical sound level but provides an effective field reduction of 80%.
evidence: This describes the sham stimulation method.

claim: Half of the patients received sham cTBS over aIFG and pIFG, respectively.
source: Half of the patients received sham cTBS over aIFG and pIFG, respectively.
evidence: This describes the counterbalancing of sham stimulation.

claim: The overall application of TMS pulses per sessions was well within safety limits and the whole procedure was in accordance with the current safety guidelines.
source: The overall application of TMS pulses per sessions was well within safety limits and the whole procedure was in accordance with the current safety guidelines (Rossi et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes safety considerations with a citation to guidelines.

claim: After a short training that did not contain any items used in the main experiments, all patients were able to perform both tasks.
source: After a short training that did not contain any items used in the main experiments, all patients were able to perform both tasks.
evidence: This describes the training procedure and patient performance.

claim: An α-level < 0.05 (two-tailed) was considered significant for all comparisons.
source: An α-level < 0.05 (two-tailed) was considered significant for all comparisons.
evidence: This describes the statistical threshold used.

claim: All statistical analyses were performed with SPSS software (version 22, Chicago, IL, USA).
source: All statistical analyses were performed with SPSS software (version 22, Chicago, IL, USA).
evidence: This describes the software used for statistical analysis.

claim: Task-related changes in the blood oxygenation level-dependent signal were analyzed with SPM 12.
source: Task-related changes in the blood oxygenation level-dependent signal were analyzed with SPM 12 (Wellcome Trust Centre for Neuroimaging; www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/) implemented in Matlab (The Mathworks, Inc, Natick, MA).
evidence: This describes the software used for fMRI analysis.

claim: All voxels lesioned in at least one patient were excluded from further analyses.
source: Note that all voxels lesioned in at least one patient were excluded from further analyses.
evidence: This describes the fMRI analysis approach.

claim: All comparisons were thresholded at an initial significance level of p<0.001, uncorrected and corrected for multiple comparisons using a p<0.05 FWE-corrected at the cluster level.
source: All comparisons were thresholded at an initial significance level of p<0.001, uncorrected and corrected for multiple comparisons using a p<0.05 FWE-corrected at the cluster level.
evidence: This describes the statistical thresholds used for fMRI analysis.

claim: Anatomical masks for the right superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) based on the Juelich Histological atlas were used to extract tract-specific FA values in each patient.
source: We used anatomical masks for the right superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) based on the Juelich Histological atlas (Bürgel et al., 2006) to extract tract-specific FA values in each patient by averaging TBSS-preprocessed, skeletonized FA data within these regions of interest (ROIs).
evidence: This describes the DTI analysis method with a citation.

claim: The choice of SLF and IFOF ROIs was based on the assumption that these tracts most likely represent the homologue tracts of the dorsal (SLF) and ventral (IFOF) pathways for phonological and semantic processing as described for the left hemisphere.
source: The choice of these ROIs was based on the assumption that these tracts most likely represent the homologue tracts of the dorsal (SLF) and ventral (IFOF) pathways for phonological and semantic processing as described for the left hemisphere (Saur et al., 2008) that should connect our cTBS sites in the left IFG with the angular and supramarginal gyrus, respectively.
evidence: This describes the rationale for ROI selection with a citation.
